ORIGINAL RESEARCH

The Value of System 1 Models in Medicine

Xiufeng Yang1,*, Konstantinos Vrettos2,*, Zeineb Ben Chaaben1, Fabian Drexel1, Jannik Lübberstedt1, Johannes Moll1, Anirudh Narayanan1, Frederike Stumpf1, Cosmin I. Bercea1, Jiawen Wang1, Evangelia E. Vassalou3, Krischan Braitsch4, Aymen Meddeb5, Sebastian Ziegelmayer1, Markus Graf1, Marcus R. Makowski1, Lisa Adams1, Nassir Navab6, Michail E. Klontzas2,3,7,+, Keno Bressem1,8,9,10,+

 

Abstract

Background Many clinical decisions are a choice among a few fixed options, taken quickly and in large numbers. Such decisions also need an uncertainty estimate to know when to defer to a clinician. Generative language models answer slowly in free text and state their confidence poorly. In contrast, System 1 models answer zero-shot with a probability for each answer. However, their performance across clinical tasks is unknown.

Methods Four System 1 models, two proprietary and two with open weights, were evaluated zero-shot on 86 public tasks from 14 clinical domains in 20 languages, spanning examination questions and medical imaging (radiography, CT and MRI). Tasks were assigned to six capability tiers before analysis. The primary outcome was the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary outcomes included calibration, language effects and comparisons with published results and generative models.

Results Across 179,111 cases, the mean AUROC of the best model per task was 0.94 for medical knowledge, 0.93 for text understanding, 0.83 for clinical judgement from text, 0.89 for image perception, 0.84 for 2D image findings and 0.69 for volumetric findings, with 0.54 for pulmonary embolism on CT. Imaging tasks scored 0.09 (95% CI, 0.06 to 0.11) lower than text tasks (P < 0.001). The best model matched or exceeded the best published result on 13 of 26 text tasks and on 8 of 35 imaging tasks. Triage nurses outperformed the best model (accuracy, 0.85 vs. 0.56). One decision took 0.34 to 0.44 seconds and 24 to 81 joules on open-weight models run locally. Accuracy on identical questions fell by up to 39 percentage points from English to Yoruba. Generative models of the same family were 11 to 76 times slower, with 3 to 5 percentage points higher balanced accuracy.

Conclusions System 1 models decide quickly, cheaply and with usable confidence when the answer is stated in a text or recalled from medical knowledge, but not when it must be judged or read from an image.

Introduction

Many clinical decisions represent choices among a few fixed options that must be made quickly and in bulk. A triage nurse assigns one of five acuity levels within minutes of arrival, a radiologist decides whether a CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrates embolism, and a coder selects one procedure code for each of thousands of cases. A model that makes such decisions must also state how certain it is, so that confident answers can be acted on and uncertain cases passed to a clinician.87; 41; 20 Generative large language models perform well on a series of medical tasks,79; 58 but they write each answer token by token, often following a reasoning trace, which takes several seconds per decision and uses far more energy than a task-specific model.53 The confidence they state in text is poorly calibrated and barely separates correct from incorrect answers.73; 59 On the contrary, System 1 models receive a state, such as a report, an image or both, together with one or more typed questions, and return a probability for every answer option in a single forward pass without generating text. Their name refers to dual-process theory, which separates fast, intuitive System 1 judgement from slow, deliberate System 2 reasoning, the mode that generative models resemble when they reason in text.36; 18

The open question is which clinical decisions such a model can be trusted with. The answer to a clinical case can be stated in a report, recalled from medical knowledge, judged from several findings, or seen in an image. Of 519 studies of large language models in health care, 44.5% tested medical knowledge such as licensing-examination questions, and 5% used real patient-care data.8 Where other tasks were tested, performance fell from more than 86% on licensing-examination questions80 to lower accuracy on real clinical cases and conversations.25; 34 On radiologic images, GPT-4V identified the imaging modality in all 515 images but detected abnormalities in 0% to 90%, depending on the finding,81 and multimodal models scored lower on volumetric than on two-dimensional images.94 If performance depends on where the answer lies, a single benchmark score misrepresents a model, a construct-validity problem known from general AI benchmarks.64

To evaluate the value of System 1 models in medicine, we tested four models on 86 tasks from 14 clinical domains, with the tasks ordered in six capability tiers from medical knowledge to volumetric findings. We measured which clinical decisions the models can take on, whether their probabilities are calibrated, how they perform outside English, and what their speed costs in time, money, energy and accuracy, against a generative model of the same family.

Methods

Study Design and Tasks

This cross-sectional evaluation used public, de-identified datasets under their respective licences. Candidate tasks came from a taxonomy of 87 clinical decision tasks in 18 domains and from further public datasets with a fixed answer format (Supplementary Appendix, Section S1). A task was included when its data and reference labels were public and its licence allowed transfer to a model hosted on a commercial API. Eighty-six tasks from 14 clinical domains met these criteria. Table S1 lists every task with the publication of its dataset. Eight of them are language versions of another task and were analysed only for language effects, which left 78 primary tasks (Figure 1). Each task used the official test split or a seeded random sample of up to 1,000 cases, in some tasks enriched for rare classes, and volumetric tasks used 81 to 436 studies. The tasks comprised 179,111 cases, with the reference standard released by the dataset authors.

Prior to result summarisation, each task was assigned to one of six capability tiers. Medical knowledge covered examination questions and terminology, text understanding covered information stated in a report, abstract or sentence, and clinical judgement from text covered decisions that integrate patient information, such as triage acuity or variant class. The three imaging tiers included image perception (acquisition, anatomy and image quality), two-dimensional (2D) image findings, and volumetric findings on CT or MRI.

System 1 Models

Four System 1 models were evaluated through the OpenRouter decision interface, each in the latest version available in October 2026. Clef (Cloudflare, 27 billion parameters) and Clef-flash (Cloudflare, 9.5 billion parameters) have open weights, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions (OpenAI) and Jev 1.14 (TypeSafe AI) are proprietary. A request held a state of text and up to four images, and one or more typed questions with a yes-or-no answer, a choice of one of nn options, or an ordered score. The model returned a probability for every option. All questions of a case were sent in one request, zero-shot, with a one-sentence description of the input. Volumetric studies were read as axial slices at a fixed spacing, with one request per slice. The study-level probability was the maximum over slices for yes-or-no questions and the mean over slices for other questions. On four 2D imaging tasks, Jev 1.14 received higher-resolution versions of the same images since its interface accepts larger images. Every request was logged as sent.

Generative Comparison

Clef and Clef-flash were compared with their generative backbones, Qwen3.8-27B63 and Qwen3.5-9B,62 and GPT-6 Luna Decisions with the generative GPT-6 Luna. The comparison covered 32 text and 2D imaging tasks. For each task, 100 randomly selected cases were sent to the generative model with the same state and questions as the System 1 model had received, including an instruction to choose one option per question, and an output schema restricted to the answer options. Default reasoning settings were kept. An answer that failed or could not be parsed counted as wrong.

Local Runs and Energy

Clef and Clef-flash were additionally run locally from the released checkpoints, on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. Local Clef’s answers were compared with the hosted versions, which confirmed that the two agreed before the local runs were utilised. Energy was measured on a sub-sample of 42 tasks and it followed the AI Research Label of the CEDARS framework for reporting the environmental footprint of clinical AI.2 The measurements come from the GPU driver’s cumulative energy counter through NVML (power usage effectiveness taken as 1.0 for a single workstation GPU). CodeCarbon (v3.3.1) ran alongside to convert energy to CO2e at the local grid carbon intensity (Greece, 337 g CO2e per kWh). Energy is reported per decision and summarised as the median and IQR over tasks. Latency was measured per request. The providers of the hosted models (GPT-6 Luna Decisions, Jev 1.14) publish no per-request energy figures for them.

Reference Results

For every task, published results on the same dataset were collected from the original dataset or challenge publication, from official leaderboards, and from a search of PubMed and the web for later work up to October 2026. Every value was checked against its source and classified as a task-specific model, a generative language model, a rule-based classifier, or clinicians and expert annotators. A published result was compared only when it used the same label set and metric on the matching questions. The highest such result per task is reported as the best published result.

Outcomes

The primary outcome was the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC), computed per question as a macro average of one-versus-rest curves for more than two options, and averaged over the questions of a task. Secondary outcomes were the balanced accuracy of the most probable option, expressed relative to chance as (BA−1/k)/(1−1/k)(\mathrm{BA}-1/k)/(1-1/k) for kk classes so that 0 is chance and 1 is perfect, the top-label expected calibration error (ECE),24; 87 selective accuracy after withholding the least confident answers,23 cost per 1,000 requests at provider prices, latency per request and energy per decision.

Statistical Analysis

Any question that a model refused or failed was scored as wrong, with the label prevalence as its probability. Task-level 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using 1,000 bootstrap resamples of cases. Task estimates were pooled within each tier and model using DerSimonian–Laird random-effects models. Two contrasts were specified in advance, imaging versus text tiers and a linear trend across the three imaging tiers, and both were estimated by random-effects meta-regression. AUROC was also summarised by question type. The accuracy of each language version on identical items was compared with English by paired bootstrap and the exact McNemar test. System 1 and generative models were compared by the mean task-level difference in balanced accuracy, with 95% CIs from a task bootstrap. Secondary analyses were not adjusted for multiplicity. Analyses used Python 3.13, pandas 3.0, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18 and scikit-learn 1.9. Code and all model outputs are available in the project repository at https://github.com/twin-x-eu/system1-models-in-medicine.

Results

Tasks and Models

The 86 tasks covered 20 languages and yielded 2.4 million model answers across 179,111 cases (Figure 1). GPT-6 Luna Decisions refused 4,008 case–question pairs (1.3%), Clef and Clef-flash each failed on one pair, and Jev 1.14 answered every question. Refused and failed questions were scored as wrong. Jev 1.14 was the best model on 45 of 78 tasks. Results per task are given in Table S2.

Capability Gradient

For the best model on each task, the random-effects mean AUROC was 0.94 (95% CI, 0.92 to 0.97) for medical knowledge, 0.93 (95% CI, 0.91 to 0.94) for text understanding, 0.89 (95% CI, 0.84 to 0.94) for image perception, 0.84 (95% CI, 0.81 to 0.87) for 2D image findings and 0.69 (95% CI, 0.60 to 0.79) for volumetric findings (Figure 2). Imaging tasks scored 0.09 (95% CI, 0.06 to 0.11) lower than text tasks (P < 0.001), and AUROC fell by 0.09 (95% CI, 0.06 to 0.13) per tier from image perception to volumetric findings (P < 0.001). Both contrasts were significant for each of the four models (Figure 2B). Clinical judgement from text reached 0.83 (95% CI, 0.73 to 0.93), lower than the other two text tiers. Chance-corrected balanced accuracy fell from 0.74 for medical knowledge to 0.20 for volumetric findings, and its trend across the imaging tiers was not significant (P = 0.10, Figure 2C).

The best model reached an AUROC of 0.99 on licensing-examination questions (MedQA)31 and 1.00 on findings stated in chest radiograph reports. On volumetric imaging it reached 0.54 for pulmonary embolism,17 0.59 for cervical spine fracture,49 0.59 for clinically significant prostate cancer72 and 0.48 for rib fracture type, and four of nine volumetric tasks stayed below 0.60. Intracranial haemorrhage on head CT reached 0.90.14 On imaging tasks, questions that assigned the whole image to one of several options reached a median AUROC of 0.87, yes-or-no questions on the presence of a finding reached 0.74, and ordered grades 0.71. On text tasks, yes-or-no questions reached 0.99.

Comparison with Published Results and Clinicians

A published result on the same dataset, label set and metric was available for 61 tasks (Figure 3). On text tasks, the best System 1 model matched (within 0.01) or exceeded the best published result in 13 of 26 tasks, with a median difference of −-0.01. On imaging tasks it did so in 8 of 35 tasks, with a median difference of −-0.17. Clinicians or expert annotators outperformed the best model in 6 of the 10 tasks for which such a comparison existed. Triage nurses assigned the emergency acuity level with an accuracy of 0.85, compared with 0.56 for the best model,54 and a points-based rule classified genetic variants with an accuracy of 0.95, compared with 0.73.66; 83 Zero-shot System 1 models are therefore competitive with purpose-built systems on text, but not on images or where a codified rule already exists.

Calibration and Selective Answering

The median top-label ECE across models was 0.05 to 0.07 on text tasks and 0.11 to 0.17 on imaging tasks (Figure 4A and 4B). On imaging tasks, GPT-6 Luna Decisions was overconfident, and about 80% of its most confident answers were correct. Withholding the less confident half of the answers raised accuracy on text tasks from between 0.76 and 0.83 to between 0.96 and 0.99, and on imaging tasks from between 0.66 and 0.70 to between 0.79 and 0.91 (Figure 4C).

Language

On the same 1,089 medical examination questions, accuracy in every language version was lower than in English for every model (Figure 4D). The decline was smallest in German and largest in Yoruba, where it ranged from 20.1 (95% CI, 17.6 to 22.5) percentage points for Jev 1.14 to 39.4 (95% CI, 36.3 to 42.4) for Clef-flash, whose accuracy fell from 0.93 to 0.54. The performance measured in English therefore overstates what these models deliver in a low-resource language.

System 1 and Generative Models

On identical cases, the balanced accuracy of each System 1 model was lower than that of the generative model of its family, by 4.3 (95% CI, 2.4 to 6.3) percentage points for GPT-6 Luna Decisions, 3.3 (95% CI, 0.0 to 6.5) for Clef and 4.8 (95% CI, 1.0 to 8.5) for Clef-flash, over 32 tasks each (Figure 5A). The difference was smaller on imaging tasks, where Clef-flash and Qwen3.5-9B differed by 0.4 (95% CI, −-1.5 to 2.3) percentage points. Each System 1 model scored higher than its generative counterpart on 8 or 9 of the 32 tasks. Generative models required a median of 4.8 to 30.3 seconds per request, compared with 0.34 to 0.44 seconds for System 1 models, and incurred 2- to 22-fold higher costs (Figure 5B and 5C).

Environmental Impact of System 1 Models

Energy was measured directly on the two open-weight models, Clef and Clef-flash, both run locally on one RTX 5090 GPU over 42 of the tasks and 117,263 decisions each (Methods). The median energy of one decision was 23.5 joules for Clef-flash (IQR, 17.2 to 51.3) and 80.9 joules for Clef (IQR, 68.4 to 125.5). That is 6.5 to 22.5 watt-hours of GPU-board energy per 1,000 decisions and, including CPU and RAM and at the carbon intensity of the local grid, 2.8 to 12.1 g CO2e per 1,000 decisions (Figure 6). Across capability tiers, the median energy per 1,000 decisions was lowest for medical knowledge (4.8 watt-hours for Clef-flash and 19.2 for Clef) and highest for text understanding (19.3 and 47.6). One kilowatt-hour buys roughly 153,000 decisions from Clef-flash and 44,500 from Clef. Decisions that included an image cost 1.6 to 2.3 times as much energy as text-only decisions, and the length of the input mattered more than its type. On the three tasks with the longest documents, the energy of a decision rose to 2.1 to 5.0 times the median for that model. The two models together took 234,526 decisions for 4.3 kilowatt-hours of GPU-board energy. The energy of a single System 1 decision is therefore small enough that it is not the limiting factor in deploying one at scale.

Local versus API Inference

Clef and Clef-flash have open weights and can run inside a hospital network, so patient data do not need to leave the institution. Run locally, they reproduced the hosted interface closely. On chest radiograph report findings, local Clef gave a mean AUROC of 0.99 equal to the version inferenced through the API, and agreed with it on 99.7% of answers, while on visual question answering, the values were 0.947 against 0.942 and 97.2% agreement.

Discussion

System 1 models answered medical examination questions and identified findings described in radiology reports with high accuracy, with inference times below half a second and for a few joules per decision. On text-based tasks, predicted probabilities were well calibrated, closely reflecting observed accuracy. However, performance declined on tasks requiring the integration of multiple findings, such as assigning acuity levels in emergency triage. On imaging tasks, they accurately identified imaging modalities and anatomical regions but frequently failed to detect specific abnormalities. Performance on volumetric CT and MRI tasks was particularly limited, approaching chance levels in four of nine tasks.

For information extraction from clinical text, the case for zero-shot System 1 models is strong. The best System 1 model matched or exceeded the best published result on 13 of 26 text tasks without any training on the task, including results from models that had been fine-tuned for that task. For the T staging of lung cancer from CT reports, the best System 1 model reached an accuracy of 0.78, compared with 0.67 for fine-tuned Japanese BERT models.55 For the pathological T stage from pathology reports, it reached an AUROC of 0.96, compared with 0.94 for a fine-tuned Clinical-BigBird model.38 A zero-shot System 1 model could therefore replace models that require task-specific fine-tuning. Each decision took less than half a second and 23.5 to 80.9 joules, with costs ranging from 0.02 to 0.16 USD per 1,000 requests. Withholding the 50% of predictions with the lowest confidence increased accuracy on text-based tasks to 0.96 to 0.99. These findings suggest that System 1 models could support large-scale report labelling, information extraction, and literature screening, while referring uncertain cases to clinicians or slower, more computationally intensive models.23; 20 Clef and Clef-flash have openly available weights and can be deployed within hospital networks.

Accuracy declined on tasks requiring clinical judgement, such as assigning triage acuity or classifying variants, even when all relevant information was provided in the input. System 1 models generate predictions in a single forward pass, relying on knowledge encoded in their weights. Unlike generative models that produce explicit reasoning traces,93 they lack intermediate reasoning steps through which multiple findings can be evaluated and integrated before reaching a decision. Across the five tasks requiring clinical judgement, the generative backbones of Clef and Clef-flash achieved accuracies 11 and 15 percentage points higher, respectively, compared with differences of 3 and 5 percentage points across all 32 evaluated tasks. Enabling System 1 models to generate reasoning traces before making predictions could help narrow this performance gap.

An additional limitation of most medical benchmarks is their predominantly English-language content. Similarly, most language models, including System 1 models, are trained primarily on English-language data.78; 57 Reflecting this, the System 1 models were most accurate in English. On the same 1,089 examination questions, accuracy fell by 2 to 7 percentage points in German, a high-resource language, and by 20 to 39 percentage points in Yoruba, a low-resource language. Generative models lose accuracy in low-resource languages in a similar manner.57; 3

Most System 1 models also accept images, but read medical images far less accurately than models trained for the task. The best System 1 model matched or exceeded the best published result in 8 of 35 imaging tasks, compared with 13 of 26 text tasks, with a median difference of −-0.17 on imaging tasks. For clinically significant prostate cancer on MRI, it reached an AUROC of 0.59, compared with 0.86 for radiologists.72 Calibration was also worse on imaging tasks, and only about 80% of the most confident answers of GPT-6 Luna Decisions were correct. Volumetric imaging was most challenging as the current interface of System 1 models accepts at most four images per request and no volumes. CT and MRI studies were therefore sent as single slices every 3 to 10 mm, and a small finding can lie between two slices. The choice of pooling rule over slices did not change the results (Supplementary Appendix, Section S6.3). Furthermore, radiographic images had to be downsampled, for example mammograms at 1,024 pixels on the long side, at which microcalcifications cover few pixels. Generative models also lose accuracy when volumes are given as image sequences,94 which indicates a property of how vision-language models process images in general.

The open-weight decision models Clef and Clef-flash are based on the Qwen family of generative models, allowing a direct comparison of the two model types. The decision models and their backbones did not differ in accuracy, however the decision models were better calibrated, with a median expected calibration error of 0.12 for Clef-flash against 0.20 for its backbone, and 0.07 for Clef against 0.13. Against the generative backbone with reasoning, the System 1 models were 3 to 5 percentage points less accurate and 11 to 76 times faster.

This study has limitations. Models were used zero-shot with a one-sentence description of the input. Task-specific prompts and fine-tuning were not tested. A System 1 model trained on the records of 3.6 million patients from one health system, CS1-4B, was recently reported to outperform open decision models of up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks in held-out patients from that system.97 Its weights have not yet been released, so it could not be included here. Public datasets can be part of the training data, which raises results on text tasks in particular. Larger frontier generative models were not tested and are likely more accurate on many tasks, but they are slower and more expensive than the generative models compared herein.

For predefined clinical decisions on text, in particular information extraction, System 1 models are ready for use, with fast, inexpensive and well-calibrated answers. They are as accurate as their backbones but better calibrated, and open weights let a hospital run them sustainably on its own data. However, they are currently limited in questions requiring clinical reasoning and in interpreting medical images, in particular CT and MRI volumes.

Appendix S1 Task Selection

The taxonomy splits radiology into five layers (acquisition and metadata, image quality, anatomy, findings, and examination or patient level). Table S1 lists the evaluated tasks.

Appendix S2 Requests

The state contained the case text as released, such as the question stem, the report sections or the triage fields, or a one-sentence description of the input together with the image. Each option of a choice question had a short description, and each level of an ordered score was described in words. Images larger than 4 MiB were downsampled by half until they were below 4 MiB. For Jev 1.14, images with a side below 280 or above 1,568 pixels were rescaled. The four 2D imaging tasks with higher-resolution images for Jev 1.14 were melanoma in ISIC 2020, paediatric pneumonia, retinal OCT and diabetic retinopathy grade in RetinaMNIST. On OpenRouter, Clef and Clef-flash were routed only to the Cloudflare provider, because another provider ignored images. When a model refused a question, the question was removed, the request was repeated with the remaining questions, and the refusal was logged. Volumetric slices were taken within the relevant body region, with the window named in the text.

Appendix S3 Scoring

For yes-or-no questions, the AUROC used the probability of the positive option. For other questions, the macro average included only the options present in the reference. Balanced accuracy was the recall of the most probable option, averaged over the reference classes. Probabilities were normalised to sum to one, because two models round probabilities to two decimals. The expected calibration error used 10 equal-width bins of the top-label probability. When a task shared its requests with another task (chest radiograph findings and view, head CT haemorrhage and critical findings), each question was counted in one task only.

Appendix S4 Generative Comparison

The generative models replied in JSON. Qwen3.8-27B answered the first 50 of the 100 cases per task. Reasoning tokens were counted and billed.

Appendix S5 Reference Results

Table S5 lists every published result with its type.

Appendix S6 Supplementary Results

S6.1  All Tasks and Models

Figure S1 shows the AUROC of every task for every model. Table S2 gives the AUROC with 95% CIs, and Table S3 the random-effects means per tier.

S6.2  System 1 Models and Their Backbones

On 20 tasks, Clef and Clef-flash were also compared with their backbones, Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.5-9B, with the backbone read out over the same options (Figure S2). Each task had one primary endpoint. The sign test across tasks was not significant for Clef-flash (better on 14 tasks and worse on 5, Holm-adjusted P=0.13) or Clef (12 and 7, Holm-adjusted P=0.36). Five of the 16 significant advantages of a System 1 model disappeared or reversed after the backbone readout was corrected for its option prior.

S6.3  Pooling of Slices

For volumetric tasks, the mean study-level AUROC of yes-or-no questions over tasks and models was 0.68 with the maximum over slices, 0.69 with the mean of the three highest slices and 0.69 with the mean over slices (Figure S3). Pulmonary embolism and cervical spine fracture stayed close to chance under every rule.

S6.4  Generative Comparison

Table S4 lists the balanced accuracy and cost of each System 1 model and its generative model per task.
